papers.title: Synaptojanin 2 is required for neuronal mRNA localization, mitochondrial structure and function, and synaptic metabolism
papers.summary: This paper investigates Synaptojanin 2, a phosphoinositide phosphatase, and shows it plays a key role in localizing specific mRNAs within neurons, particularly at synapses. Loss of Synaptojanin 2 disrupts mitochondrial shape and function, impairing local energy metabolism at synaptic sites. These findings connect RNA localization machinery to mitochondrial health and synaptic metabolic support in neurons.
papers.why: The study's focus on mitochondrial structure, function, and synaptic metabolism in neurons directly informs mechanisms relevant to mitophagy and metabolic regulation that could be probed spatially in interneurons and perineuronal net-associated circuits.
papers.figure: Figure showing mitochondrial morphology and functional measurements (e.g., membrane potential or respiration) in neurons with Synaptojanin 2 loss versus control.

papers.title: Drug Repurposing of Rapamycin Mitigates Amyloid-β-Associated Proteotoxicity in Caenorhabditis elegans Models of Alzheimer’s Disease
papers.summary: This paper tests whether rapamycin, an already-approved drug known to activate autophagy, can reduce toxic effects of amyloid-beta protein buildup in C. elegans worm models of Alzheimer's disease. Rapamycin works by inhibiting mTOR, a cellular pathway that normally suppresses autophagy and mitophagy, so its activation can help cells clear misfolded proteins and damaged mitochondria. The study likely shows that this drug repurposing approach reduces amyloid-beta-related toxicity and improves disease-related phenotypes in the worm model.
papers.why: This supports the project's focus on autophagy and mitophagy as therapeutic targets for neurodegenerative proteotoxicity, relevant to understanding mechanisms that may also apply to neuronal and interneuron health in Alzheimer's-related brain pathology.

papers.title: Intracellular delivery of specific autophagy-inducing peptides by genetically engineered bacteria boosts host immune responses.
papers.summary: This paper describes engineered bacteria designed to deliver specific autophagy-inducing peptides directly into host cells. The approach uses bacteria as a vehicle to trigger autophagy, which in turn enhances the host's immune response. This represents a synthetic biology strategy for manipulating autophagy pathways to boost immunity, potentially relevant for vaccine or infection control applications.
papers.why: While focused on immune cells rather than neurons, this work demonstrates peptide-based autophagy induction mechanisms that could inform strategies for selectively triggering mitophagy/autophagy in specific neuronal populations like interneurons.

papers.title: Autophagy induction by cytoplasmic Acinus requires Lrrk activity
papers.summary: This study investigates how the protein Acinus, when localized in the cytoplasm, triggers autophagy, the cell's process for recycling damaged components. The researchers found that this autophagy induction specifically depends on the activity of Lrrk (Leucine-rich repeat kinase), a gene whose human homolog LRRK2 is strongly linked to Parkinson's disease. The abstract suggests a mechanistic pathway connecting Acinus localization and Lrrk kinase function to the regulation of autophagic processes.
papers.why: Since Lrrk2 mutations are a major genetic cause of Parkinson's disease affecting neuronal health, understanding Lrrk-dependent autophagy mechanisms could provide molecular insight relevant to mitophagy and autophagy dysregulation in neurons, a core focus of this PhD project.

papers.title: Emerging Single-Cell and Spatial Transcriptomics: From Multi-Kingdom Interactions to Genetic Variation and Population Diversity.
papers.summary: This paper discusses emerging trends in single-cell and spatial transcriptomics technologies, covering applications that span multi-kingdom biological interactions, genetic variation, and population diversity studies. It appears to be a broad review-style article highlighting methodological advances rather than a focused experimental study. The abstract is generic and does not specify brain tissue, neurons, or particular disease contexts.
papers.why: Although not neuron-specific, this review could offer useful methodological updates on spatial transcriptomics platforms and analysis approaches that may be adaptable to studying interneurons and perineuronal nets in brain tissue.

papers.title: Mitophagy receptor OPTN alleviates renal fibrosis via ubiquitinated TOMM22.
papers.summary: This paper investigates how OPTN, a receptor protein involved in mitophagy (the selective clearance of damaged mitochondria), helps protect kidneys from fibrosis. The researchers found that OPTN works by recognizing ubiquitinated TOMM22, a mitochondrial outer membrane protein, to tag damaged mitochondria for removal. This process appears to reduce scarring and damage in kidney tissue, suggesting mitophagy is protective in this disease context.
papers.why: Although focused on kidney rather than brain tissue, this study provides mechanistic insight into OPTN-mediated mitophagy receptor function and ubiquitinated TOMM22 signaling, which could inform how similar mitophagy pathways operate in neurons and interneurons within the PhD project's scope.
papers.figure: A figure showing the proposed model of OPTN-TOMM22 interaction and mitophagy pathway in renal fibrosis would be most informative for understanding the mechanistic parallels to neuronal mitophagy.

papers.title: Methylophiopogonanone B Alleviates Hypoxic Pulmonary Hypertension by Modulating Mitophagy via SRC.
papers.summary: This paper investigates Methylophiopogonanone B, a natural compound, as a potential treatment for hypoxic pulmonary hypertension, a disease caused by low oxygen levels damaging blood vessels in the lungs. The researchers found that this compound works by regulating mitophagy, the process cells use to clear out damaged mitochondria, through a protein called SRC. By modulating this pathway, the compound helped reduce the severity of pulmonary hypertension in their experimental models.
papers.why: This paper is only tangentially relevant, as it explores mitophagy regulation by a pharmacological agent in lung vascular cells rather than neurons, interneurons, or brain tissue, but the mitophagy mechanisms described could offer conceptual parallels.

papers.title: Cistanche deserticola exosome-like nanoparticles alleviate constipation through PINK1-dependent mitophagy and gut microbiota remodeling
papers.summary: This paper studies exosome-like nanoparticles derived from the plant Cistanche deserticola and shows they can relieve constipation in a model system. The mechanism involves activating PINK1-dependent mitophagy, a process where damaged mitochondria are selectively cleared from cells, along with changes to the gut microbiota composition. Together these effects improve gut motility and function, suggesting a plant-derived nanoparticle therapy for digestive issues.
papers.why: While focused on gut rather than brain tissue, this paper is relevant because it provides mechanistic insight into PINK1-dependent mitophagy regulation by natural nanoparticles, a pathway directly applicable to studying mitophagy dysfunction in neurons.
